Solid State Physics · Properties of Solids

Module II — Theory of solids

Theory notes: concepts, results and what every symbol means

Free electron theory

in one lineTreat the metal's loose electrons as a gas of tiny balls. It explains conduction — but gets heat capacity wrong by a factor of 100, because it ignores the Pauli principle.

The Drude–Lorentz picture

A metal is a rigid array of positive ion cores with the outer (valence) electrons set loose to wander. The model assumes:

  • Electrons move freely; the ion cores just sit there.
  • Electrons ignore each other (no repulsion).
  • The potential inside is flat and constant, taken as zero — so an electron's energy is purely kinetic. This is the assumption that eventually breaks everything.
  • Outside is higher potential, so electrons stay trapped inside the metal.
  • They behave like an ideal gas — but charged, and enormously denser than air ( per ).
  • Lorentz treated that gas with ordinary Maxwell–Boltzmann statistics.

Three successes, four failures

What it gets right:

  1. Ohm's law. With no field the motion is random and there is no current; apply a field and the electrons drift, scattering as they go, giving a steady current proportional to voltage.
  2. Wiedemann–Franz law. The same electrons carry both charge and heat, so the ratio is the same constant for every metal at a given temperature.
  3. Optical properties. Opacity and metallic shine — the electrons absorb the incoming wave, oscillate, and re-radiate it.

What it gets wrong:

  1. Resistivity vs temperature. Predicts ; experiment says .
  2. Electronic heat capacity. Equipartition gives every electron , predicting per mole. Measurements give about 1% of that, and it grows linearly with .
  3. Magnetic susceptibility. Predicts a strong (Curie) behaviour; the real thing is small and almost temperature-independent.
  4. Mean free path. Cannot explain why, at low temperature, an electron travels past – atoms without scattering.
where marks get lost

All four failures share one cause: wrong statistics. Maxwell–Boltzmann lets every electron soak up thermal energy; the Pauli exclusion principle does not. Sommerfeld fixes the first three by switching to Fermi–Dirac statistics. The fourth needs the periodic lattice — and that is band theory.

Fermi energy & friends

in one lineTrap electrons in a box, fill the levels two at a time from the bottom. The energy of the topmost filled level is the Fermi energy , and it depends only on the electron density.

Density of states

in one line counts how many electron levels sit in each slice of energy. In 3-D it grows as , which makes the average electron energy .

What D(E) means and what it is

The density of states is simply: how many available levels lie between energy and . It matters because anything electrons do — absorb heat, conduct, get excited — depends on how many states are available to move into.

Fermi–Dirac & heat capacity

in one lineThe Fermi function says a level is occupied with probability . Warming a metal only disturbs a thin sliver of width around — which is why is tiny and grows linearly with .

The Fermi function

whereFermi–Dirac function: probability that a state of energy is occupiedenergy of the stateFermi level, where Boltzmann's constantabsolute temperature

Read it as: the chance that a level of energy actually has an electron in it. That in the denominator is the whole difference from classical statistics — it is what stops the probability ever exceeding 1, i.e. it is Pauli exclusion written as a formula.

  • At it is a perfect step: below , above. Everything is filled to the brim and nothing above.
  • At the step softens over a width of about , and — worth memorising — at every temperature.
  • itself barely moves with temperature: .

The Fermi level moves (slightly) with temperature. Above 0 K, is no longer the top filled level but the level that is occupied with probability . It falls a little as rises:

whereFermi energy at temperature Fermi energy at 0 Kthermal energy; it is tiny next to , so the shift is very small

Because in a metal, the correction is tiny and is usually taken as . Only electrons within about of (a fraction at room temperature for eV) can be excited.

Why the electronic heat capacity is so small

Both failures of the classical model are cured at once: the size is right, and the linear temperature dependence is right.

Band gaps & Bloch

in one linePut the electron in a repeating potential instead of a flat one. Bragg reflection at the zone boundary opens gaps, and Bloch's theorem says the wavefunction is a plane wave times a lattice-periodic ripple.

Where the gaps come from

The free-electron model cannot explain three things: why solids split into conductors, semiconductors and insulators; why the Hall coefficient is sometimes positive; and why semiconductor resistivity falls as it warms.

The culprit is the flat-potential assumption. A real electron travels through a repeating row of positive ion cores, so the potential repeats too:

wherepotential energy of an electron at position lattice period; the potential repeats after every

Once it repeats, an electron wave can Bragg-reflect off it — exactly as an X-ray does. That happens when

wherewave number at which Bragg reflection happens and an energy gap opensnon-zero whole numberlattice period

At those the forward and reflected waves are equally strong and combine into standing waves. Two standing waves are possible: one piles the electron charge on top of the positive cores (lower energy, more attraction), the other piles it between them (higher energy). No state exists in between — and that missing range of energies is the band gap.

learn this by heart

Gaps open at , the Brillouin zone boundaries, because that is where Bragg reflection turns travelling waves into standing waves.

Bloch's theorem

The theorem tells you the shape any wavefunction must have in a repeating potential:

whereBloch wavefunctionplane wavewave numberfactor with the same period as the latticelattice period

In words: a plane wave (the free-electron part) multiplied by a ripple that repeats with the lattice. The electron still travels through the crystal; it just gets modulated as it passes each atom.

How the proof runs (enough to reproduce the argument):

  1. The equation is second order, so it has two independent solutions and . Because repeats, the shifted functions and must also be solutions, so they are combinations of and .
  2. Requiring that shifting by only multiplies by a constant, , gives a determinant condition — a quadratic in .
  3. The Wronskian is the same at and , which forces the constant term of that quadratic to be . So .

Two cases follow, and this is the punchline:

  • Roots complex, : then with real , giving — exactly the Bloch form. The wave stays finite everywhere. These are the allowed bands.
  • Roots real, : then grows without limit at one end, so it cannot be normalised and is unphysical. These are the forbidden gaps.

Kronig–Penney

in one lineA solvable repeating potential. One equation, whose left side must stay between and — inside that range you get an allowed band, outside it a gap.

The model and its one equation

Replace the real potential with a row of square wells and barriers of period : zero inside the well of width , height across the barrier of width . Solve in each region, apply Bloch's theorem, match the wavefunction and its slope at the boundaries, and set the resulting determinant to zero.

Reading bands and gaps off it

Here is the trick that makes the whole model work. The right-hand side is a cosine, so it can never leave the range to . A real value of therefore exists only when

wherebarrier strength, a dimensionless measure of the energy cannot go beyond , so only energies where the left side stays within exist: allowed bands. The rest are gaps.

Energies satisfying that are allowed; energies where the left side escapes the range are forbidden. Plot the left side and the band structure simply appears.

The two limits — very commonly asked:

Also: as energy rises, the factor shrinks the oscillation, so bands get wider and gaps get narrower.

How the bands are drawn, and how many electrons fit

Since repeats every , is periodic in -space. Three standard ways to draw it: the extended scheme (band drawn in zone ), the reduced scheme (everything folded back into the first zone), and the periodic scheme (repeated in every zone). Same information, three pictures.

One band holds exactly electrons, where = number of primitive cells. One valence electron per atom → band half full → metal. Two per atom → band exactly full → insulator, unless bands overlap.

Effective mass & classification

in one lineAn electron in a band responds to a field as if it had a different mass — which can even be negative. A full band carries no current at all.

Speed and effective mass

An electron in state is really a wave packet, and it travels at the group velocity:

wheregroup velocity of the electron (speed of the wave packet)band energy as a function of wave numberreduced Planck constantangular frequency,

So the slope of the band gives the speed. At the bottom of a band () and at the zone boundary () the slope is zero, so — those are the standing waves again. The speed peaks in between, at the point of steepest slope.

Reading off a band — the practical version

You are never asked to compute from first principles; you are asked to read it. Three rules cover every question:

  • Curvature is everything. , so a sharply curved band means a light, responsive electron and a flat band means a heavy, sluggish one. Narrow bands (weakly overlapping atomic orbitals) therefore give large effective masses — that is why -band electrons in transition metals are heavy.
  • Bottom of a band: small and positive. Here and the electron behaves exactly like a free particle that happens to have the wrong mass. This is the region that matters for a semiconductor’s conduction band.
  • Top of a band: negative. The curvature has flipped, and the electron accelerates against the applied force. This is the region that matters for holes.

In between, at the inflection point , the curvature passes through zero and formally diverges — the electron there refuses to accelerate at all, because the lattice takes back exactly as much momentum as the field supplies.

  • Lower half of the band: curvature positive → , the electron accelerates the way you push it.
  • At the inflection: curvature zero → , the field cannot change its speed at all.
  • Upper half: curvature negative → . The electron accelerates backwards.
where marks get lost

Negative mass looks like nonsense but breaks nothing. is a bookkeeping trick that hides the lattice force: the electron really feels both the applied field and the lattice. Near the top of a band the lattice force (Bragg reflection handing momentum back to the crystal) beats the applied force, so the net acceleration opposes the field — and we record that as . Total momentum, electron plus lattice, is conserved throughout.

Holes

A nearly full band with one electron missing is far easier to describe by tracking the vacancy instead of the remaining electrons. Because the missing electron sat where is negative, the vacancy — a hole — behaves as a real particle with

whereeffective masses of the missing electron and of the holewave vectors of the missing electron and of the holetheir velocitiescharge of the hole,

A positive charge with a positive mass. This is what makes the Hall coefficient come out positive in some materials — something free-electron theory could never explain.

Metals, semiconductors, insulators

First the key result: a completely full band carries no current. Summing the contributions of all its electrons gives a total proportional to evaluated at the zone boundary — and that slope is zero. So no matter how hard you push, a full band contributes nothing. Conduction requires a partly filled band.

learn this by heart

The one-line test. A solid conducts if and only if there is an empty level immediately above an occupied one. Partly filled band, or two bands overlapping → metal. Full band with a big gap above it → insulator. Full band with a small gap above it → semiconductor, which is an insulator at and a conductor when warmed.

  1. Insulator — full valence band, empty conduction band, wide gap –6 eV (diamond). Thermal energy cannot lift electrons across. Essentially no conduction.
  2. Semiconductor — same picture but a narrow gap, eV (Si , Ge eV). At it is an insulator. Warm it and electrons hop the gap leaving holes behind, with whereconductivity of the intrinsic semiconductorband gapBoltzmann's constanttemperature — conductivity rises steeply with temperature.
  3. Metal — a partly filled band (one electron per atom filling half of the capacity), or two bands that overlap (the alkaline earths). Empty states sit right next to filled ones, so conduction is easy. Here : warming adds lattice vibrations that scatter electrons more.
